slides.text: My job at the Metropolitan Opera Gala pays a hundred dollars a night and has one rule: wear a rented tuxedo, don't speak to the celebrities, and whenever a billionaire gets up to visit the champagne bar, slip into their velvet chair so the rows never look empty on camera. By 9:00 PM, I had been a temporary duke, a temporary senator, and a temporary oil baron.

At 9:15, I was ushered into Table Four beside a woman in an emerald silk gown who looked like she was drowning in pearls. Her fiancé—a hedge-fund heir—had gone to work the room, and he didn't come back for forty minutes. She immediately kicked off her heels under the tablecloth, stole the cherry from my water glass, and whispered, 'If you tell me one more thing about municipal bonds, I’ll jump into the orchestra pit.'

So I told her about my cramped studio apartment in Queens, my three-legged cat, and how I learned to fold napkins into swans at catering gigs. She laughed harder than anyone at the ten-thousand-dollar tables. When her fiancé finally returned, I stood up to vanish into the crowd—but she stood up too, unclipped her diamond bracelet, left it on his bread plate, and took my hand. 'Come on,' she smiled. 'I hear Queens has better pizza.'
